statement: In adults entering one US residential research unit to come off opioids, 30 people whose urine showed fentanyl (enrolled 2021 to 2024) compared with 103 people who entered about a decade earlier with other opioids such as heroin (2010 to 2015), all given the same fixed morphine treatment (only the fentanyl cohort could also have other medicines for symptoms), were associated with more withdrawal while on that treatment: their self-rated withdrawal rose to a peak in the first days and then eased, while the earlier group's fell steadily from the first day; on four of the days severe self-rated withdrawal was 3 to 6 times as common (for example 47% against 8%); observers rated most of the fentanyl group as mildly withdrawn on most days against a small minority of the earlier group, though almost no one in either group was rated above moderate; and 43% against 19% had a fast heart rate at least once. Anxiety, aches, stomach symptoms, sweating and many other symptoms were all higher, with no single symptom explaining the difference. The comparison group came from another decade and another trial, the fentanyl group was older and could be given extra comfort medicines, ratings were not blind, and xylazine and other adulterants were not tested, so fentanyl cannot be shown to be the cause; the study also measured withdrawal during morphine treatment, not untreated withdrawal. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People coming off illicit fentanyl in one research unit had worse withdrawal than people coming off heroin there ten years earlier, even though both got the same medicine. Their withdrawal got worse over the first days before easing, and fast heartbeats were more common. Because the two groups were from different times and the fentanyl group got extra medicines, we cannot be sure fentanyl itself caused the difference.

comparator: Urine positive for other opioids, no fentanyl, at entry about a decade earlier (2010 to 2015), with the same fixed morphine treatment on the same unit
outcome: Self-rated (SOWS) and observer-rated (COWS) withdrawal, its course over the stabilization days, heart rate, blood pressure and pupil size
magnitude: No effect sizes or confidence intervals reported. Severe self-rated withdrawal, fentanyl against earlier cohort: 48% against 16%, 47% against 8%, 37% against 6% and 27% against 6% on four consecutive days; observer-rated mild withdrawal 73% against 33% up to 73% against 18% on the following days; tachycardia at least once 43% against 19% (p < 0.05). Peak self-rated scores higher on five of seven days (SOWS model F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01); observer-rated on six of seven days (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001); the abstract gives one day fewer for each.

statement: In emergency responders such as police officers and paramedics, evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how often, incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues on the skin causes opioid toxicity (an overdose): no source on file measured responders' exposure or blood levels or counted poisonings among exposed responders, and none of the four, a position statement and three descriptive studies, documents a confirmed case. A 2017 position statement of two North American clinical-toxicology societies, the American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology (AACT) (Moss et al., 2017: eight authors from poison centres, universities, hospitals and a public health institute in the USA and Canada; the recommendations rest on the opinion and clinical experience of a task force of ACMT members and a literature search by the authors; reviewed by an ACMT committee, its board and its members and approved by both societies' boards; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; filed here as a narrative review, so its figures are second-hand and no search method is given), measured no exposure, blood level or responder, and says that its recommendations mainly represent the consensus opinion of experts because data are limited. The two societies judged the risk of clinically significant exposure for responders to be extremely low, and incidental absorption through the skin unlikely (in the recommendations, very unlikely) to cause opioid toxicity. They wrote that they had not seen reports of responders developing signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact, and that the reports they cite (a 2016 warning of the US Drug Enforcement Administration, with two 2017 news reports cited for responders' concern) described nonspecific symptoms, such as dizziness or a feeling that the body was shutting down, without objective signs such as slowed breathing; the incidents are not examined one by one and no count of exposures is given, so the statement could not have detected how often poisoning happens. Their reasoning is arithmetic for fentanyl, not measurement: with both palms covered by fentanyl skin patches, which are made to deliver the drug, about 14 minutes would be needed to absorb 100 micrograms, an amount the statement treats as a high dose without saying why it was chosen (editors' check: 425 micrograms an hour at the stated steady-state rate); they argue that powder or tablets on the skin are taken up more slowly than from a patch and can be brushed or washed off, so that toxicity, if it occurred, would not develop rapidly. At the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, an unprotected person would need nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed), and the statement says that fentanyl's very low vapour pressure suggests evaporation from standing powder is not a practical concern. Splashes to the eyes or mouth are treated as a real route (absorption across mucous membranes more than 30 times that across skin, as stated; one case report of a veterinarian who became drowsy after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, where the authors say the part played by carfentanil is unclear). No estimate is given for carfentanil, described as 10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals, or for any other analogue, although the conclusions cover them; the statement says that the analogues' physical properties suggest a potential for skin absorption and that pharmacological data on other analogues are limited. It concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. It holds that toxicity cannot occur from simply being near the drug, and it still recommends nitrile gloves for routine handling, washing skin with water rather than with alcohol-based sanitizers, and, in the unusual case of significant airborne powder, a properly fitted N95 respirator or P100 mask, which it judges likely to give reasonable protection (its summary says an N95 gives sufficient protection in exceptional circumstances with drug particles or droplets in the air); it adds that individual practitioners may differ. The first data, all descriptive, also find no confirmed case, and none could have found how often one occurs. A review of news reports (Herman et al., 2020: eight authors from an emergency medicine department at Johns Hopkins University, published as an editorial in the journal that carried the position statement, with the statement's last author as its senior author; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared) searched LexisNexis for English-language print and online news from North America published from January 2012 to March 2018: of 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 were on the topic and 214 described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid, and none of the 214 described a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together. Only one incident, in 2016, mentioned any laboratory test of an exposed responder, a urine result reported as traces of opiates, which the authors explain probably came from an opiate screen, a test that does not detect fentanyl or its analogues and, in urine, reflects exposure over the previous several days rather than at the time. The unit is the article, not the incident (distinct incidents are not counted), each article was read by one of five reviewers against criteria the paper does not define, and only the three-part combination is reported, so the zero shows that the news did not report confirmation, mainly because testing was almost never mentioned, not what happened to the responders. A Health Hazard Evaluation by the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH; Jackson et al., 2018) reconstructed one incident in early 2018 from records and from interviews four months later: during a vehicle search, white powder from a locked box blew into the faces of two officers, who within minutes reported difficulty breathing, dizziness and confusion, and a colleague gave one of them naloxone for what was described as shallow breathing and fading consciousness; emergency medical services then found both alert and oriented with normal oxygen saturation, and in the emergency department both had normal-sized pupils and normal heart and breathing rates, neither had any laboratory test, and both went home after more than an hour without symptoms. A field test of the seized substances was reported positive for fentanyl, but the state forensic laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC and no fentanyl or other opioid. Nothing was measured on the officers or in the air, the powder reached their faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and their perceived risk was not assessed; the clinicians who examined them saw no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity, and NIOSH considers it possible that the non-specific symptoms reflected milder toxicity from some drug. In the same report NIOSH states, as its own position and citing the position statement among its sources, that a brief touch of fentanyl powder, or of an analogue, is not expected to be toxic when visible powder is quickly removed. A later NIOSH article (Chiu et al., 2019: seven NIOSH authors, two of whom also wrote that report; no funding and no conflicts of interest declared; read as its author manuscript) summarizes two other incidents that NIOSH investigated, from 2017 and 2018, chosen to illustrate different scenarios; neither is the incident of that report. In the first, during a traffic stop, wind blew powder from a container onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, who cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer; within 5 minutes the officer felt disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision, and ambulance staff washed the skin with water and found the officer alert, with pupils of 4 mm, a breathing rate of 17 a minute and raised blood pressure and heart rate; no laboratory test was done, the officer was discharged with an assessment of chemical exposure, and the laboratory later found fentanyl with methamphetamine in the powder left in the container. In the second, four officers became lightheaded or dizzy, among other symptoms, after a call to a hotel room with drug powders in view: three who had entered the room, about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began, and one who never entered, 30 to 45 minutes after handling a camera and other items from the room that showed no visible contamination; one officer slumped to the ground and improved rapidly after a colleague gave naloxone; none was reported to have depressed breathing (one officer's breathing rate ranged from 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department), all were alert with no documented constricted pupils, and their urine screens, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative; the laboratory found fentanyl, a fentanyl analogue, heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones in the room. Nothing was measured in the air, on surfaces or skin, or in blood, and perceived risk was not assessed. The authors judge that no officer's effects were consistent with severe opioid toxicity, consider breathing in, the lining of the eyes, nose or mouth, swallowing and the skin all possible routes, and read the one officer's improvement after naloxone as suggesting that opioids played a substantial part, an inference from one uncontrolled observation in an officer whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; like NIOSH's report, they state that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic when visible contamination is promptly removed, and they add that alcohol-based hand sanitizer may increase absorption. None of these studies can show that no responder has ever been poisoned: news reports are a selected record in which testing was almost never mentioned, and three incidents, investigated because officers fell ill, give no rate. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (for the absence of a confirmed case only).
plain: In 2017, two North American societies of poison specialists said that an emergency responder, such as a police officer or paramedic, is very unlikely to be poisoned by brief, accidental contact with fentanyl on the skin. They had seen no reports of a responder with signs of an opioid overdose from such contact; the reports they cite described dizziness and similar feelings, without signs such as slowed breathing. Their view is expert opinion backed by arithmetic, not measurement: even with both palms covered in fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver the drug, it would take about 14 minutes to take in what they treat as a high dose. Powder splashed into the eyes or mouth is treated as a real risk, and no arithmetic was done for stronger analogues such as carfentanil. They still recommend gloves, washing skin with water, and a fitted mask when powder is in the air. The first real-world data point the same way but cannot settle it. In 214 news stories from 2012 to 2018 about police officers or paramedics exposed to opioids, none described a likely route, symptoms that fit an opioid overdose and a confirming lab test together; only one incident mentioned any test, a urine screen that probably cannot detect fentanyl. The stories were counted rather than the incidents, and one reviewer read each. In one incident looked into by a US federal workplace-safety agency, powder blew into two officers' faces in 2018 and they felt ill; their medical records showed no signs of a serious opioid overdose, neither was tested, and although a field test said fentanyl, the lab found cocaine and methamphetamine but no fentanyl or other opioid in the seized drugs. The agency says a brief touch of fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic if visible powder is quickly removed. In two more incidents the same agency looked into, five officers felt dizzy or unwell; in one, powder later found to contain fentanyl and methamphetamine blew onto an officer in short sleeves. One officer slumped to the ground and recovered quickly after naloxone, which the agency's authors read as a sign that an opioid played a part. The agency judged that none had signs of a serious opioid overdose, and no officer had a test that can detect fentanyl, so these cases can neither confirm nor rule out poisoning. None of these studies can show that no responder has ever been poisoned.
population: Emergency responders (law enforcement and emergency medical services) in North America who may meet fentanyl or fentanyl analogues as powder, tablets or liquid on calls, at crime scenes or in drug raids: as considered in a 2017 position statement, which studied no responders, exposures or cases; as reported in 214 English-language North American news articles (January 2012 to March 2018) that described a specific responder's exposure to an opioid; and two sheriff's department officers in one incident in early 2018, investigated afterwards by NIOSH, and five police officers in two other incidents of 2017 and 2018, also investigated afterwards by NIOSH (Chiu et al., 2019)
exposure: Incidental contact with fentanyl or its analogues: on the skin (the question here), and also airborne powder breathed in, splashes to the eyes or mouth, and being near the drug; reasoned from pharmacokinetic data in the position statement, as reported in news articles (routes recorded but not reported), and, in the NIOSH incident, white powder of unknown composition blown into two officers' faces; in the two incidents of Chiu et al., powder blown onto an officer in short sleeves and without gloves, which the laboratory later found to contain fentanyl with methamphetamine, and a hotel room with drug powders in view, with items from it handled elsewhere; no source measured any exposure
comparator: None in any source: the position statement collected no data, and its worked arithmetic takes as its reference the time needed to absorb 100 micrograms of fentanyl through the skin, or the exposure needed to reach a dose of 100 micrograms from the air, an amount it does not justify; the news review and the incident investigations had no comparison group
outcome: Clinically significant opioid toxicity in the responder (objective signs such as slowed breathing or a lowered level of consciousness), as distinct from nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness or anxiety; in the news review, a confirmed exposure (an article describing a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together); in the NIOSH incidents, symptoms and clinical findings in emergency medical service and emergency department records (with urine drug screens, unable to detect fentanyl, in four officers), and forensic analysis of the substances seized
magnitude: No measured rate or count of poisonings. ACMT and AACT position (Moss et al., 2017): risk of clinically significant exposure extremely low; no reports seen of responders with signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact; incidental skin absorption unlikely (summary) or very unlikely (recommendations) to cause toxicity. Worked arithmetic, fentanyl only: both palms covered by fentanyl patches (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%, delivery 2.5 micrograms per cm2 per hour at steady state), about 14 minutes to absorb 100 micrograms (editors' check: 170 cm2 × 2.5 = 425 micrograms an hour, so 14.1 minutes); patches take 3–13 hours to give a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 hours to peak; at the highest airborne concentration met by industrial workers, nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 micrograms (inputs not stated, nor whether inhaled or absorbed); vapour pressure 4.6 × 10^-6 Pa. Mucous membranes: more than 30-fold the absorption of skin; one case report of drowsiness after a splash of carfentanil with xylazine, its cause unclear to the authors. No estimate for carfentanil (10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals) or any other analogue. Respiratory protection: an N95 respirator or P100 mask likely to give reasonable protection against significant airborne powder (recommendations); an N95 sufficient in exceptional circumstances with particles or droplets in the air (summary). Herman et al. (2020), English-language North American print and online news (LexisNexis), January 2012 to March 2018: 1,408 articles retrieved, 1,016 relevant (editors: 72%), 214 describing a specific responder exposure (editors: 21% of relevant); 0 of 214 with a plausible route, consistent symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing together; any laboratory testing of an exposed person mentioned for 1 incident (2 articles; editors: 0.9% of 214), an opiate urine result; distinct incidents not counted, and no count reported for any single criterion. Jackson et al. (2018; NIOSH), 1 incident, 2 officers: no laboratory test of either officer; no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity in EMS or emergency department records (alert and oriented, normal oxygen saturation, normal-sized pupils, normal heart and respiratory rates in the emergency department, blood pressure raised); observed for more than an hour and discharged; naloxone given to one officer at the scene; seized items: cocaine, methamphetamine and THC identified, alprazolam and sodium bicarbonate only indicated, no fentanyl or other opioid, against a presumptive field result for fentanyl; no exposure measured. Chiu et al. (2019; NIOSH), 2 incidents, 5 officers: no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl (HHE 1, no laboratory test; HHE 2, urine screens negative for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates, with cut-offs of 500 ng/mL for amphetamines and 150 ng/mL for cocaine; opiate screens do not detect fentanyl); HHE 1: onset within 5 minutes; first vital signs blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17, heart rate 105, pupils 4 mm and reactive; later heart rate 80–85, breathing rate 15–21, blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104; powder left in the container 1.56 g, fentanyl and methamphetamine identified; HHE 2: onset about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began for the three officers who entered the room and about 30 to 45 minutes after handling items for the fourth; one dose of intranasal naloxone to one officer, with rapid improvement; no depressed breathing reported; one breathing rate of 9 to 20 a minute in the emergency department; hotel-room evidence: fentanyl 0.14 g, heroin 0.14 g, N-ethylpentylone 2.87 g, para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl, dibutylone, and cocaine and methamphetamine residues; no exposure measured; perceived risk not assessed.

evidence.extracted: Fentanyl is amenable to absorption through the skin (low molecular weight, lipophilic); depending on the product, fentanyl patches take 3–13 h to produce a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 h to reach peak concentration; absorption of liquid fentanyl increases with larger area, longer application, broken skin and heat; analogues have similar physical properties, suggesting potential for dermal absorption, and in a small volunteer study sufentanil under an occlusive dressing was absorbed comparably to fentanyl, exact bioavailability not determined. Incidental dermal absorption is unlikely to cause opioid toxicity: if both palms were covered with fentanyl patches it would take about 14 min to receive 100 mcg of fentanyl (body surface area 17,000 cm2, palm surface area 0.5%, absorption 2.5 mcg/cm2/h), an extreme example said to show that even fentanyl prepared for delivery through the skin cannot rapidly deliver a high dose. The calculation, from patch data, overestimates exposure from tablets or powder, which need surface area, moisture and dissolution and lack a patch's delivery matrix and adhesive; the 2.5 mcg/cm2/h figure is a steady-state rate after the drug has penetrated the dermis and overestimates absorption in the first minutes, when drug seen on the skin can be removed by brushing or washing with water. So small unintentional skin exposures to tablets or powder are judged very unlikely to cause significant opioid toxicity, and toxicity, if it occurred, would not develop rapidly. risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_moss_2017 (editors' narrative-review checklist): overall high. The evidence was chosen by a task force after a literature search with no stated databases, dates, terms or criteria; the recommendations are, in the statement's own words, primarily consensus expert opinion; the absence of poisoned responders is the authors' observation, without a search record, a case series or a count of exposures; the incidents are represented by a DEA warning and news reports and are not examined one by one. Card sc_herman_2020 (JBI prevalence checklist, first pass): moderate for what the count describes, whether news articles reported a confirmed exposure: each article coded by one reviewer against undefined criteria, with no agreement statistic, distinct incidents not counted, and results given only for the three-part combination. Card sc_niosh_2018 (JBI checklist, first pass): high for any conclusion about cause: no biological, air or skin sample, a field test contradicted by the laboratory, no record of which item formed the cloud of powder, and an account reconstructed four months later. Card sc_chiu_2019 (JBI checklist, first pass): high for any conclusion about cause: two referred incidents chosen to illustrate scenarios, reconstructed weeks to months later, with nothing measured on the officers or around them and no test able to detect fentanyl. All four share one gap, the absence of any measurement of exposure, so one level, not two.

inconsistency.note: None: the position statement (from its authors' knowledge), the news review and the three incidents investigated by NIOSH all report no confirmed case; they differ in design and none estimates a rate.

indirectness.note: Second-hand and extrapolated in the position statement: the skin estimate uses fentanyl patch data, a steady-state rate through a matrix designed to deliver the drug, which the authors themselves say overstates uptake from powder or tablets; the air estimate uses industrial exposure data whose inputs are not given; both are for fentanyl only, with no figure for carfentanil or other analogues; the 100-microgram reference amount is not explained; and the statement concerns responders' incidental contact, not people who handle or use fentanyl regularly. The news review examined news text, not medical, police or laboratory records. In the NIOSH incident the powder reached the officers' faces and one officer's nose, not only their skin, and no opioid was identified in the seized items, so it bears on reported exposures in general, not on skin contact with fentanyl. In the first incident of Chiu et al. the powder, which contained methamphetamine as well as fentanyl, blew onto the officer and the uniform outdoors in wind, so breathing it in or contact with the eyes, nose or mouth are not excluded; in the second the officers were in or near a room with scattered powders and residues; neither bears on skin contact alone.

imprecision.note: Not rated separately: no source estimates a rate or count of poisonings among exposed responders (the news review counts articles, not exposures or incidents, and the three investigated incidents have no denominator), a gap already counted under risk of bias; very low is the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. The news review describes the media's own selection (incidents that reached English-language news indexed by LexisNexis); that selection is counted under risk of bias and indirectness, not here.

statement: In police officers and other emergency responders in the United States, surveyed at trainings in Missouri in 2019 (Winograd et al., 2020) and Indiana in 2020–2021 (del Pozo et al., 2021) and online in New York State in 2019 (Persaud & Jennings, 2020), and interviewed at five law enforcement agencies in 2020 (Attaway et al., 2021), the belief that touching fentanyl can cause an overdose, or in New York that briefly touching it could be deadly, was held by about 4 in 5 of those surveyed, and concern about it was voiced by nearly all of those interviewed who were asked; answers given just after a training that included a 10-minute module correcting it disagreed with it far more often, but these before-and-after comparisons, with no comparison group or later follow-up and many participants missing, cannot show that the training changed the belief, or for how long. The studies measured what responders believed and said, not what fentanyl does: whether touching fentanyl can cause an overdose is a separate question (see 'Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?': evidence insufficient, no confirmed case on file), and the papers call the belief false or misinformation on the strength of the 2017 position statement of two clinical-toxicology societies and similar sources, not their own data. Before a 2-hour overdose-response training in the Eastern Region of Missouri (11 sessions, January to August 2019, reaching 200 participants, of whom 140 were analysed: 113 law enforcement or security officers and 27 emergency medical or fire department workers), 20.9% answered False to the True/False item "I can overdose from touching fentanyl." (law enforcement 16.8%, 19 of 113; emergency medical 37.0%, 10 of 27; 29 of 140, 20.7%, by the editors' arithmetic), so about 4 in 5 did not. Before a 3-hour harm-reduction and occupational-safety training (SHIELD) held by Zoom for Indiana officers from December 2020 to June 2021 (204 attendees from 49 counties, of whom 129, 63.2%, answered the baseline survey), 103 of 129 (79.8%; Wilson 95% interval about 72% to 86%, editors' calculation) agreed, 52 of them strongly, with a 6-point item saying that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it; 79 of the 129 (61.2%) had earlier had fentanyl exposure precaution training. Neither sample was random: both were attendees of trainings in one Midwestern state each, answering a single unvalidated item. In an online pilot survey of police, fire and emergency medical workers serving New York State (Persaud & Jennings, 2020: February and March 2019; spread through 3 of 15 associations asked, flyers and personal contacts, so no response rate can be known; 187 analysed of 247 responses), 149 of 187 (79.7%; about 73% to 85%, editors' calculation) agreed with a statement that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: 86 of 92 in law enforcement (93.5%) and 63 of 95 in fire, emergency medical services or both (66.3%); the six answer levels are reported only as agree or disagree, so slight and strong agreement cannot be told apart. Asked where they got information on fentanyl exposure and safety (all that apply), most named seminars or courses (78.1%) and department training (76.5%), 67.4% federal agencies and 13.9% news media, but no answer was linked to its source, and the authors' suggestion that overreliance on media reports lies behind the belief rests on no analysis. In interviews at five purposively chosen agencies (January to May 2020; 23 officers and leaders analysed, 20 of them asked open questions about fentanyl), nearly all of those asked said they were concerned that encountering fentanyl might put them at risk of an overdose and a few were not, with no counts given for any theme; they named other officers, law enforcement professional organizations, a Drug Enforcement Administration roll-call training video shown at in-service training (released in 2016 according to Attaway et al.; Herman et al., 2020, give the same video, at the same Justice Department web address, as of 6 June 2017), and regional intelligence bulletins as their sources; over one third of officers had heard of someone in their own agency overdosing, but none could say for certain that the substance was fentanyl or that the colleague had overdosed; two said they had been exposed themselves without symptoms; and a handful who were asked did not know the toxicology societies' statement. The interview study's abstract, saying that nearly all those interviewed wrongly believed skin contact was deadly, is sharper than its Results. In online US news found through Media Cloud for January 2015 to September 2019 (Beletsky et al., 2020), 506 of 551 relevant articles (92%) were coded as misinformation, a category that included any article giving an anecdotal account of an overdose blamed on casual contact, with its rumoured symptoms, so neutral incident reports counted, against 45 corrective or partially corrective articles, 18 of them unequivocally corrective; misinformation articles received 450,011 Facebook shares, against 48,235 for the corrective or partially corrective and 29,652 for the unequivocally corrective (about 15 to 1 against the last group, the abstract's figure, and about 9 to 1 against all 45, editors' calculation); the authors' potential reach of 69,751,705 is shares multiplied by an assumed 155 contacts, an upper bound on views, not a count of people, although the abstract presents it as people reached; and the two most-shared stories, as the authors summarize news reports, concerned two Ohio officers, one whose powder and overdose were never confirmed by laboratory testing and one whose substance was later confirmed as methamphetamine. Counting articles and shares cannot show that the coverage shaped officers' beliefs. Immediately after the Missouri training, which included about 10 minutes on contact with fentanyl, 83.6% answered False (law enforcement 81.4%, emergency medical 92.6%; 117 of 140 by the editors' arithmetic), so about 1 in 6 did not; of the 69 Indiana officers (53.5% of baseline respondents, 34% of attendees) who completed a follow-up linked to their baseline, 27 (39.1%; about 28% to 51%, editors' calculation) still agreed and 42 (60.9%) disagreed, 22 of them strongly, and their mean score moved from 2.2 to 4.0 on the scale from 1 (strongly agree) to 6 (strongly disagree) (paired t = 6.52, p < .001). Neither study had a comparison group or a later follow-up; the second answers came after the trainers had given the answer, from people who knew what was wanted; 43 of the 200 Missouri participants are unaccounted for and no paired counts are reported; two-thirds of the Indiana attendees are missing from its before-and-after comparison, whose abstract sets 79.8% of 129 against 39.1% of 69; and any change belongs to the whole training, not to the 10-minute module alone. The Indiana paper's printed effect sizes are wrong: its Cohen's d of 2.33 for the change is incompatible with its t and n, and by the editors' calculation the standardized change is about d_z = 0.78, the printed 2.33 matching the standard deviation of the paired differences and the printed interval [1.05, 0.51] matching that of d_z rather than that of the 1.8-point mean change (about 1.25 to 2.35). The two training studies share two authors (Goulka, Beletsky), and Beletsky is also first author of the media study; the trainings were developed or are delivered by the authors' teams, and both evaluations were publicly funded (in Missouri through the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, in Indiana through a CDC Overdose Data to Action grant); the New York survey, by two authors at John Jay College of Criminal Justice with no funding beyond administrative support, shares no author with them. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (for the share holding the belief, now found by independent teams; the answers after training come from one team only).
plain: In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police officers and other emergency workers thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose, or could kill: before training, 103 of 129 Indiana officers agreed that responders are at great risk of overdose from touching or breathing it in (2020–2021), and only about 1 in 5 of 140 Missouri police and ambulance or fire workers said it was false that they could overdose from touching it (2019). In an online survey in New York State in 2019, 149 of 187 police, fire and ambulance workers agreed that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: about 9 in 10 police and 2 in 3 of the others. Most named courses and department training as where they got information about fentanyl safety, and about 1 in 7 named the news; the survey did not ask which source the belief came from. None of these surveys picked people at random. In interviews at five US police forces in 2020, nearly all officers asked said they were worried; they named other officers, a training video from the US Drug Enforcement Administration (one paper dates it 2016, another June 2017) and police bulletins as where they had heard it, and over a third had heard of a colleague overdosing, though none could say it was confirmed. Researchers counted 506 of 551 US news articles from 2015 to 2019 as misinformation, including plain reports of officers falling ill; these got about 450,000 Facebook shares, against under 30,000 for articles that clearly corrected it. Right after trainings that included a 10-minute lesson on fentanyl, far fewer still agreed: about 1 in 6 in Missouri, and 27 of the 69 Indiana officers who answered again. But nobody compared trained with untrained people or asked again later, many never answered a second time, and the Indiana paper printed its effect sizes wrongly. These studies show what people believed, not what touching fentanyl does.
population: Police officers and other emergency responders in the United States: 140 responders analysed (113 law enforcement or security officers and 27 emergency medical or fire department workers; mean age 40.96, 110 men) of 200 people reached by 11 overdose-response trainings in the Eastern Region of Missouri, January to August 2019; 129 of 204 Indiana officers from 49 counties who attended three SHIELD trainings held by Zoom between December 2020 and June 2021 and answered the baseline survey (mean age 45.1, 97 men), 69 of whom also answered the follow-up; 23 officers and agency leaders at five purposively chosen US law enforcement agencies, interviewed from January to May 2020, 20 of them asked about fentanyl; 187 New York State police, fire and emergency medical workers (92 in law enforcement; 95 in fire, emergency medical services or both) who answered an online pilot survey in February and March 2019, of 247 responses; and, for news coverage, 551 online US news articles from January 2015 to September 2019

comparator: None outside the trainees: the same people's answers just before the training (in Missouri everyone analysed, with no paired counts reported; in Indiana the 69 linked completers); no untrained comparison group and no later follow-up; in the news study, corrective and partially corrective articles against misinformation articles; in the New York survey, none (law enforcement and fire or emergency medical workers are reported side by side)
outcome: Answers to single belief items (True or False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl, in Missouri; agreement on a 6-point scale with an item that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, in Indiana; agreement on a 6-point scale, reported only as agree or disagree, with a statement that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, in New York); concern about overdose from encountering fentanyl and the sources named, in interviews, and the information sources ticked in the New York survey; for news articles, the authors' coding as misinformation, corrective or partially corrective, Facebook shares and modelled potential views

evidence.extracted: SHIELD (Safety and Health Integration in the Enforcement of Laws on Drugs) is a training programme for law enforcement on harm reduction and occupational safety, covering needle-stick injuries, officer mental health, the public safety benefits of harm reduction programmes and of treatment for substance use disorders, and a 10-minute module on fentanyl exposure. Three 3-hour sessions were held in Indiana by Zoom in December 2020 and March and June 2021, led by a former police officer. grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3): it reports how many responders said they held the belief, where they said it came from, how news coverage carried it, and how answers differed just after a training; it does not claim that training changed beliefs, which these designs cannot show. Descriptive, observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias (training attendees and a self-selected online sample rather than random samples, heavy missing data, single unvalidated items, second answers given straight after the corrective message, interviews without counts) and one for indirectness (two Midwestern states, New York State and five agencies in 2019 to 2021; items about overdose, and in New York about death, one combining touching with inhaling; answers rather than behaviour): very low. Not upgraded: descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect, and the before-and-after shifts are not estimates of an effect. Rated as worded: as estimates of a training effect, both training studies are at critical risk of bias under ROBINS-I (no comparison group, an immediate post-test, attrition), so a claim that training changes the belief would also be very low, and the statement says that the designs cannot show it. The single quotation records the Missouri item itself, because its wording is the measure; the Indiana item, 17 words long, is paraphrased. Editors' calculations (Wilson intervals; counts from the printed group percentages; the recomputed standardized effects, d about 0.40 and 0.56 and d_z about 0.78; the interval for the paired change; the ratios of shares) are labelled for the second reader to recompute. Printed figures corrected or qualified: the Missouri overall 20.9% fits 29 of 139, not of 140 (20.7%), and its differences are percentage points; the Indiana Cohen's d values (2.33, 1.61, 2.33) are incompatible with the printed t and group sizes, its paired interval matches d_z rather than the mean change, and its printed patrol means contradict the stated direction; the Indiana abstract's 79.8% against 39.1% mixes denominators of 129 and 69 and calls a 3-hour training with a 10-minute module a 10-minute online training; the news study's 6.6% of total is 6.6% of misinformation shares (6.0% of all), and its 70 million people reached are an upper bound on views; and the interview study's abstract says more than its Results. statement: In the United States, law-enforcement seizure records and overdose death records describe counterfeit pills taking a growing part in fentanyl exposure from 2018 to 2021, comparing the first with the last quarter of each period; neither source tested what share of pills sold on the street contain fentanyl. In quarterly records from the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas programme (33 designated trafficking areas, in 50 states and the District of Columbia, whose participating federal, state, local and tribal agencies report their seizures), seizures in which any fentanyl or fentanyl analogue was detected rose between January–March 2018 and October–December 2021 from 424 to 1,539 for powders and from 68 to 635 for pills. Pills were thus 13.8% of these pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures at the start and 29.2% at the end (68 of 492 and 635 of 2,174, editors' calculation); the authors' conclusion that 'over a quarter of fentanyl seizures are now in pill form' refers to this share of seizures, not to the share of pills that held fentanyl. The number of fentanyl-containing pills seized in a quarter rose from 42,202 to 2,089,186, partly because pill seizures grew larger (about 621 pills per pill seizure at the start and about 3,290 at the end, editors' calculation). Read from the figures, all four counts were higher in April–June or July–September 2021 than in the last quarter, while the pill share was at its highest in the last quarter. The records hold nothing on what the pills were made to look like, how much fentanyl they held, what else they contained or where in the country the changes happened, and seizures reflect policing, testing and reporting as well as supply, which the authors acknowledge (Palamar et al., 2022). In death records from 30 jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia) in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System, the share of unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use was 2.0% in July–September 2019 and 4.7% in October–December 2021 (106,293 deaths over the period), after a high of about 5.1% in April–June 2021 (read from the figure); in the eight western jurisdictions it went from 4.7% to 14.7%, their highest quarter, and it stayed below 4% in the other regions. Evidence of counterfeit pill use meant any of: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit; pills that tested positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; pills that looked like oxycodone or alprazolam when that drug was absent on post-mortem toxicology; unmarked pills; or a witness report of pill use when no drug detected exists as a legitimate pill. It was coded from death-investigation narratives; how many pills were tested in a laboratory is not reported; the authors expect it to be undercounted, unevenly within and between jurisdictions; and some pills found at a scene may not have been used. In 2021, in 35 jurisdictions, 2,437 of 54,768 overdose deaths (4.4%) had such evidence: of counterfeit oxycodone only in 1,346 (55.2%; pills marked 'M-30' documented in 889 of them), of counterfeit alprazolam (Xanax) only in 415 (17.0%, editors' calculation), of both in 95 (3.9%) and of an unspecified type in 581 (23.8%, editors' calculation); 55.8% of them were in western jurisdictions, against 16.3% of other overdose deaths. Illicitly manufactured fentanyls were listed as a cause of 93.0% of the deaths with such evidence against 72.2% of other overdose deaths, and as the only drugs listed (alcohol not counted) in 41.4% against 19.5%; illicit benzodiazepines in 5.3% against 1.4%, and in 17.1% of the deaths with evidence of counterfeit alprazolam only. These are drugs listed as causes of death, not the contents of tested pills; the authors infer that the pills used likely contained the drugs that caused death (O'Donnell et al., 2023). The one drug-checking study read, at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver in 2017–2018, tested mostly powders and very few pills (no number given) and reports no results by form, so it gives no figures for pills (Tupper et al., 2018). How well fentanyl test strips detect fentanyl is a separate answer (see the answers on fentanyl test strips). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are fake pills with fentanyl getting more common? In the US up to 2021, two kinds of records say yes, though neither tested what share of street pills hold fentanyl. Of police seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021; the rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months went from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million, partly because seizures got bigger. In death records from 29 states and Washington, DC, the share of overdose deaths with signs that fake pills were used went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to about 5 in 100 by mid-2021 and then stayed about there; in western states it went from about 5 to about 15 in 100. In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes of 93 in 100 of them. Police seizures depend on what police look for and test, death records probably miss many fake pills, and a drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say anything about them.
population: Fentanyl-containing drug seizures recorded by law-enforcement agencies taking part in the 33 US High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (50 states and the District of Columbia), 2018–2021; unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths with a medical examiner or coroner report in 30 US jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia), July 2019 to December 2021, and in 35 jurisdictions in 2021; and samples brought for drug checking at two supervised consumption sites in Vancouver, Canada, 2017–2018
exposure: Pill form, against powder form, among fentanyl-containing seizures; documented evidence of counterfeit pill use among overdose deaths
comparator: The first against the last quarter of each period, with no statistical test of the death-record trend; for 2021, overdose deaths without such evidence in the same jurisdictions; census regions
outcome: Quarterly counts of fentanyl-containing powder and pill seizures, the pill share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures and the number of pills seized; the quarterly share of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use, the pill imitated and the drugs listed as causes of death

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could materially change the figures. The seizure series depends on which agencies reported and what they tested, neither of which is described, and on policing priorities, and it is reported only at its first and last quarters (card sc_palamar_2022: JBI, moderate as a description of recorded seizures, high as an indicator of supply). Evidence of counterfeit pill use in deaths depends on how completely death investigators documented pills, which the authors expect to vary within and between jurisdictions, rarely rests on pills known to have been tested, and may have been documented more fully as awareness of counterfeit pills grew, which would inflate the rise (the editors' concern, not tested; card sc_odonnell_2023: JBI moderate).

inconsistency.note: The two record systems agree in direction; they measure different things, and the statement does not compare their sizes.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: records of seizures and of deaths with documented evidence, not the contents of pills sold on the street, which the statement says neither source tested; US only, to 2021.

imprecision.note: Large record sets (hundreds to thousands of seizures a quarter; 106,293 and 54,768 deaths); no intervals are printed, but chance is not the main concern.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for surveillance series; not suspected.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (counts, shares and their change over time in records): starts low, is never upgraded, and is downgraded one level for risk of bias because coverage and measurement could materially change the figures (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias are not downgraded. Very low. Status replicated: two independent record systems, run by different teams, agree in direction (pills became a larger part of US fentanyl seizures in 2018–2021, and deaths with evidence of counterfeit pills a larger share of overdose deaths in 2019–2021); each figure comes from one source, the two measure different things and their sizes cannot be compared, and O'Donnell et al. cite Palamar et al. without sharing its data. Both are compared first quarter against last quarter, and in both the counts or the total share peaked in mid-2021, which the statement says. The drug-checking study qualifies the claim only by showing that it cannot answer for pills. Nothing here measures the share of street pills that contain fentanyl, how much they hold, or the risk of using a counterfeit pill; the DEA laboratory figures on pill contents that Palamar et al. cite were not read and are not used.
